solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: It has circle, it has rings! (6)

indicatorNotes.has: the first piece holds on to the second, so they sit side by side

blocks.note: 'it' is old slang for sex appeal, abbreviated SA
to circle is to go round, to turn

annotation.surface: An excited cry about something round and ringed, like a hoop or a target.
annotation.walkthrough: Both 'it's read as pronouns; the first is the old slang for sex appeal ('she's got it'), while the second half, 'it has rings', is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: this planet is the one best known for its bright ring system.

entries.clue: Drink and flirt? (8)

blocks.note: a thick blended fruit drink
a flirt as a person: a slick, silver-tongued charmer

annotation.surface: Someone at a bar wonders whether to order a drink and chat somebody up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flirt' is a noun here, a person who flirts, which is what lets it match a smoothie in the smooth-talker sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A smoothie is both a blended fruit drink and an informal word for a slick, charming man.

entries.clue: Blunted needles applied to joint, immediate and painful punishment (5,5,5)

indicatorNotes.applied to: the needles are put next to the joint, so the pieces sit side by side

blocks.note: something blunted has been cut short
sharps = needles, as in a hospital sharps bin
the hock is the ankle joint of a horse's hind leg

annotation.surface: A grim scene of blunt needles being stuck into a joint as some cruel, swift penalty.
annotation.walkthrough: The split runs across the words of the answer: SHARPS gives the S that starts SHOCK. 'Short, sharp shock' is a British phrase for a brief, harsh punishment, famously for young offenders.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a short, sharp shock is a quick, severe punishment meant to deter.

entries.clue: Book opened by English and Greek character, classic example (7)

indicatorNotes.opened by: the E and PI come at the start of the book, opening it

blocks.note: E = English
pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
a tome is a large book

annotation.surface: A classic book whose first page begins with English and Greek writing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Book' comes first in the clue but last in the answer: being 'opened by' the other pieces puts it at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word names the one instance that sums up a whole type perfectly.

entries.clue: Not the winner, though hardly puffing? (5,3,2,5)

annotation.definition: Not the winner, though hardly puffing?

blocks.note: reads as a plain runner-up; really one who nearly won
reads as not out of breath; really not smoking the prize

annotation.surface: A runner-up who finished without even being out of breath.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Puffing' pretends to mean panting from effort, but it is puffing on a cigar, the old fairground prize a near-miss didn't win.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom said of an attempt that nearly succeeds but just falls short of the prize.

entries.clue: Ultimately impressive, say, property bequeathed (6)

indicatorNotes.Ultimately: in the end, so take the final letter

blocks.note: last letter of impressivE
to state = to say

annotation.surface: Someone remarks on an impressive inheritance of property.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Say' reads as 'for example' in the surface; it is really the verb to state.
annotation.definitionFit: An estate is all the property a person leaves to be passed on at death.

entries.clue: Unidentified humanoid in spirit eyed up (4)

indicatorNotes.in: the answer sits inside the next words
indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, reading upward turns the letters round

blocks.note: spirIT EYed
reversal indicator: in a down clue the letters are read upward

annotation.surface: An unknown creature is glimpsed by someone who has been drinking spirits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' is a natural hint at a ghost, but it only carries letters here.
annotation.definitionFit: The yeti is the unconfirmed ape-like creature said to roam the Himalayas.

entries.clue: Symbol of victory in hand? (4)

annotation.definitionNote: 'in hand' points to a part of the hand rather than the whole

blocks.note: winners in ancient games were handed a frond from this tree
the flat inner surface of the hand

annotation.surface: A winner holding a trophy in their hand.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the loose second half: the palm is a part of the hand rather than a synonym for it.
annotation.definitionFit: Palm fronds were given to victors in ancient times, and the palm is the flat inside of the hand.

entries.clue: Swinging joint (3)

blocks.note: swinging = fashionable, as in the swinging sixties
a joint of the body, at the top of the leg

annotation.surface: A joint that swings, like a hinge or a limb.
annotation.walkthrough: Read together, 'swinging joint' sounds like a hinge or a lively nightclub; split, it is two separate meanings of HIP.
annotation.definitionFit: Hip means trendy, like 'swinging', and it is also the ball-and-socket joint at the top of the leg.

entries.clue: Look here where inlets forming (6)

indicatorNotes.forming: the letters are being formed into something new

blocks.note: anagram fodder

annotation.surface: A guide points to a spot on the coast where small bays are taking shape.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Look here' is not about seeing: it is the interjection that demands attention, just as 'Listen!' does.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Look here!' and 'Listen!' are both said to make someone pay attention.

entries.clue: Jokes I’m not sure written in time (6)

indicatorNotes.written in: the UM is written inside the HOUR

blocks.note: an hour is a unit of time
um is the noise of hesitation

annotation.surface: A comedian pencils in some jokes at the last minute, doubtful they will land.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I'm not sure' is a whole phrase standing for the hesitant sound UM.
annotation.definitionFit: Humour means jokes and comic material in general.

entries.clue: Island state, like isle I observed in word of gratitude (8)

indicatorNotes.observed in: the pieces are seen inside the word of thanks

blocks.note: ta = thanks, informal British
as = like
the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea
I as itself

annotation.surface: A traveller says thank you on arriving at an island state that resembles another island.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Island state' reads as a nation like Malta; here it is a state within a federal country. Everything between 'Island state,' and 'in' goes inside the thanks.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: this island off the south of Australia is one of that country's six states.

entries.clue: Air’s beneath them circulating, at once (2,3,4,6)

indicatorNotes.circulating: moving round, so the letters are stirred

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters

annotation.surface: Air moves beneath birds' or planes' wings as they fly.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'Air's' is ignored; its S is part of the fodder. Air and breath make the surface quietly fit the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to say two things in the same breath is to say them at once.

entries.clue: Greek letter, that afore upsilon, originally (3)

indicatorNotes.originally: take each word at its origin, its first letter

blocks.note: That Afore Upsilon

annotation.surface: A description of a Greek letter as the one coming just before upsilon.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is true: the answer is the letter just before upsilon in the Greek alphabet.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: one particular Greek letter, the one the rest of the clue places before upsilon.

entries.clue: Cat – or weasel, by the sound of it? (7)

indicatorNotes.by the sound of it: judge by how it is spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: a weasel is a sly, cheating person; CHEATER said in a non-rhotic accent

annotation.surface: Someone can't tell whether an animal is a cat or a weasel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Weasel' wants to be another animal next to 'cat'; it is really a sly, untrustworthy person, a cheater.
annotation.definitionFit: The cheetah is the big cat famed as the fastest land animal.

entries.clue: Success impacted (3)

blocks.note: a smash success, as with a chart-topping song
impacted = struck, the past tense of a verb of striking

annotation.surface: A success that made a real impact.
annotation.walkthrough: The two words are different parts of speech: 'Success' is a noun, 'impacted' a past-tense verb, and one short word covers both.
annotation.definitionFit: A hit is a success, and hit also means struck or impacted.

entries.clue: Being discussed, a number of lies? (2,5)

blocks.note: A as itself
from the set phrase for a web of falsehoods, 'a ___ of lies'

annotation.surface: A debate in which several untruths come up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A tissue of lies' is a set phrase for a web of falsehoods, so a tissue is a collection of lies.
annotation.definitionFit: A matter at issue is the one under discussion or in dispute.

entries.clue: He philosophised like that over cases (8)

indicatorNotes.over: in a down clue, the SO sits above the CRATES

blocks.note: so = in that way
crates are packing cases

annotation.surface: A thinker argues his point in exactly that way over several cases.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cases' sounds like legal or philosophical arguments; they are packing boxes.
annotation.definitionFit: Socrates was the Athenian philosopher famous for questioning people.

entries.clue: Damaging plug, number of lines (7)

blocks.note: a plug is a bit of advertising, an ad
a verse is a group of lines in a poem

annotation.surface: A harmful advertisement written as a few lines of poetry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plug' reads as a stopper; it is the verb-turned-noun for promoting something.
annotation.definitionFit: Adverse means harmful or damaging, as in adverse effects.

entries.clue: Poor introduction from Stevenson, Kidnapped? (8,3,4)

indicatorNotes.introduction from: the opening letter of the word

blocks.note: first letter of Stevenson
a kidnap victim is trapped for cash, held to ransom

annotation.surface: A reader finds the opening of Robert Louis Stevenson's novel Kidnapped disappointing.
annotation.walkthrough: Kidnapped is Stevenson's novel, but here it is the plain verb: someone kidnapped is held, trapped, for a ransom in cash.
annotation.definitionFit: Being strapped for cash means being short of money, poor.

entries.clue: Wales is windy, and centre of England too (2,4)

indicatorNotes.is windy: winding, twisting, so the letters move
indicatorNotes.centre of: the centre of a word is its middle, so take the letter at the heart of ENGLAND

blocks.note: WALES rearranged
the middle letter of engLand

annotation.surface: A weather report: it's blowy in Wales and in the Midlands too.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Windy' pretends to be weather; it means winding. ENGLAND has seven letters, so its centre is the fourth, L.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean in addition, tacked on at the end of a sentence.

entries.clue: Proust lost in brain fog (6)

indicatorNotes.lost: the letters have lost their way

blocks.note: anagram fodder

annotation.surface: Marcel Proust, the novelist of memory, drifting in a mental haze.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface nods to Proust's In Search of Lost Time, a novel all about memory.
annotation.definitionFit: A stupor is a dazed state where the mind is fogged.

entries.clue: When so, so devious, is it something akin to a racket? (8)

indicatorNotes.devious: going by a winding route, so the letters wander

blocks.note: anagram fodder

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether a shady scheme counts as a racket.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Racket' pretends to be a scam; it is the tennis kind. A snowshoe is a racket-shaped frame strung with webbing, worn to walk on snow.
annotation.definitionFit: Traditional snowshoes are frames with laced webbing, much like a tennis racket.

entries.clue: Bread that also may rise? (4)

indicatorNotes.that also may rise: in a down clue it can be read upward and still be the bread

blocks.note: in a down clue, reading upward gives the same bread

annotation.surface: Bread that can puff up in the oven, like a risen loaf.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rise' is the baking word, but here it means reading upward: NAAN reads the same bottom to top.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a leavened flatbread from South Asian cooking.

entries.clue: Reckless winger invariably costing Arsenal, result uplifting Spurs, initially (6)

indicatorNotes.initially: take the initial letter of each word

blocks.clueFragment: invariably costing Arsenal, result uplifting Spurs, initially
blocks.note: Invariably Costing Arsenal, Result Uplifting Spurs

annotation.surface: A football report: a careless wide player keeps giving away games for Arsenal, to the delight of rivals Spurs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Winger' is a football wide player in the surface; in the answer it is someone with wings. Arsenal and Spurs (Tottenham Hotspur) are rival north London football clubs.
annotation.definitionFit: Icarus flew on wax wings and recklessly soared too near the Sun.

entries.clue: Bulb I left in bank, screwed back (6)

indicatorNotes.in: I and L go inside the bank
indicatorNotes.screwed back: twisted round backwards, so the whole thing is reversed

blocks.note: a crag is a steep rocky bank
I as itself
L = left
reversal indicator: twisting it back turns C(IL)RAG round

annotation.surface: Someone planting a bulb in a riverbank and twisting it back into the earth.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bulb' sounds like a light bulb screwed into a socket, but it is a plant bulb, the kind split into cloves.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a head of this plant is a bulb made up of cloves.

entries.clue: Country dropping off in spring (3)

indicatorNotes.dropping off: letting something fall away from the end

blocks.note: the country
IN is dropped off the end

annotation.surface: Someone in the country nodding off in the springtime.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link word; it is the letters taken away. 'Spring' is a water source, not the season.
annotation.definitionFit: A spa is a mineral spring, or a resort built round one.

entries.clue: Some lover, ostensibly? (4)

indicatorNotes.Some: only some of the letters are used

blocks.note: lovER OStensibly

annotation.surface: Someone who appears to be in love, at least on the face of it.
annotation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue also defines: the god of love is 'some lover' on the face of it, and the question mark admits the stretch.
annotation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of erotic love, a lover par excellence.
